newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's biggest company drops on profit warning.
newsitem.headline: Australia's biggest company drops on profit warning.

text.p: Australia's largest company, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, on Monday saw about A$760 million (US$580 million) wiped of its market capitalisation after warning of lean times ahead.
Investors abandoned the blue chip "Big Australian" in response to a one-page statement to the Australian Stock Exchange early on Monday.
The statement foreshadowed a flat performance until it restructured and new projects were commissioned.
At one point, BHP shares were down 57 cents before recovering to close 40 cents lower at A$18.92.

SBC James Capel analyst David Irons said BHP was sold down aggressively initially on the profit warning but had come back in later trade as investors took a more sanguine view of the overall strategic review.
BHP said there were some one-off items that would impact adversely on the company and that trading conditions remained difficult.

BHP managing director John Prescott later in the day told reporters any substantial profit contributions from new projects in zinc, diamond and platinum mining, steelmaking and mineral sands are a year or more away.
"The fourth quarter is likely to have an outcome that seems to be below what some people assume it will be," Prescott said, referring to the last quarter of BHP's year ending May 31, 1997.
By May 1998, BHP plans to commission new projects with capital value of A$3.1 billion, he said.
Additional new contributions valued at A$2.3 billion are earmarked for the following year.
But there is little to soothe the bottom line in the short term.
"Other things are too small to have a big impact this year ... that's why we see this flat situation extending into next year," Prescott said.
"You are not going to see it (profit from new projects) in early '98,"
Prescott reaffirmed BHP's commitment to operating a diverse range of businesses amid some criticism it was spreading itself too thin, saying it was important due to cyclical commodities markets.
BHP's steelmaking division is operating at capacity , but under pressure at home and abroad, he said.

In copper, where BHP is ranked the world's second largest producer, with mines and plants in Chile, Peru, Papua New Guinea and North America, a drive to cut costs is underway amid international price pressures, Prescott said.
Acknowledging difficulties in the copper market, BHP sees a average metal price of only US$1 a pound this year compared with the current spot price of around US$1.18.
This is hardly a vote of confidence in the fundamentals of the market, analysts noted.
At the Magma Copper division in the U.S., there are efforts to cut production costs by 10 cents a pound, Prescott said.
In petroleum, robust business just a few months ago have given way to softer conditions, which Prescott expects to prevail over the medium term.
"That means some margin pressure everywhere," Prescott said.
Prescott said BHP also would drop the group's internal performance target of a 15 percent return on equity and instead focus on measuring itself against companies it deems to be on a peer level.

"The objective of the company is to perform at a level that's in the upper 20 percent of companies against which it is appropriate to compare itself, both in terms of its ongoing performance and in terms of growth," Prescott said.
He said to expect an all-encompassing writedown when full year results for the year ending May 31 are tallied next month rather than eking out abnormal items over time.
Monday's sell down in BHP shares followed a recent surge that swept the company's shares up by 16 percent since they hit a low of A$16.45 on April 14.
